sources.label: ChromeStatus feature record 5179328935624704 — Pseudo target on events (the URL the page links in the at-a-glance table and the see-also list). As fetched 2026-10-06 from the record API: browsers.chrome.status.text 'Proposed', is_released false, intent_stage 'None', flag false, origintrial false, chrome desktop/android/webview all 147, ff and safari views 'No signal', bug_url https://issues.chromium.org/issues/40639103, spec_link https://github.com/w3c/uievents/pull/413/changes; its summary states '.pseudoTarget that is either CSSPseudoElement ... or null', 'The events are UIEvent, AnimationEvent, TransitionEvent', and 'mouseover, mouseout, mouseenter, mouseleave and their pointer* counterparts are not yet supported'.

CSS Pseudo-Elements Level 4 editor's draft, §7.1 CSSPseudoElement Interface — the WebIDL for the object pseudoTarget returns: readonly CSSOMString type, readonly Element element, readonly (Element or CSSPseudoElement) parent, readonly CSSOMString selectorText, pseudo(). As fetched 2026-10-06 the draft contains zero occurrences of 'pseudoTarget', 'UIEvent' or 'AnimationEvent', so it defines the returned type but not the property itself.

MDN: CSSPseudoElement (linked from the page's see-also list) — member descriptions for the object pseudoTarget yields: element 'Returns the ultimate originating Element of the pseudo-element' (read only), type 'Returns the pseudo-element selector as a string' (read only). As fetched 2026-10-06 the page does not mention pseudoTarget.

inventory.name: pseudoTarget event property — read-only, UA-set; present on UIEvent, AnimationEvent and TransitionEvent instances; yields the CSSPseudoElement the event was dispatched on (type = the pseudo-element selector such as '::before', element = the originating DOM element) or null when the event was not dispatched on a pseudo-element, with Event.target unchanged in both cases; mouseover/mouseout/mouseenter/mouseleave and their pointer* hover counterparts are documented as not yet supported

syntax.rationale: FLAGGED — forced-documented dimension with no declaration grammar to earn it. pseudoTarget is a read-only property the UA sets on event objects; an author never declares it, so there is nothing to write, and #the-pseudotarget-property carries no <pre><code> block, no WebIDL, no CSS declaration and no option dictionary — it states the surface in one sentence, a three-item bullet list and inline <code> only: the property is carried by UIEvent, AnimationEvent and TransitionEvent, it is a CSSPseudoElement whose type is the pseudo-element selector and whose element is the originating DOM element when the event was dispatched on a pseudo-element, it is null otherwise, and Event.target is unchanged. The nearest real grammar in the cited sources is the CSSPseudoElement WebIDL in css-pseudo-4 §7.1, which defines the returned object's members rather than pseudoTarget itself; the only form a reader actually types (event.pseudoTarget.type) sits in the #detecting-a-click-on-after example. This instance is reported as a page that cannot express the schema's forced syntax:documented rule honestly, not dressed up as a grammar.

inputs.rationale: The fragment enumerates the incoming events that carry the property: a table of UIEvent (click, pointerdown, focus, keydown), AnimationEvent (animationstart, animationend, animationiteration) and TransitionEvent (transitionstart, transitionend, transitionrun), followed by the note that mouseover, mouseout, mouseenter, mouseleave and their pointer* hover counterparts are not yet supported. The condition for a non-null value — the event having been dispatched on a pseudo-element — is stated in the bullet list at #the-pseudotarget-property.

outputs.rationale: The bullet list in this fragment states both possible results: a CSSPseudoElement whose type is the pseudo-element selector (e.g. '::before') and whose element is the originating DOM element, or null; plus that Event.target remains the originating element in both cases, so no existing output changes.

errors.rationale: No error surface exists to document: this fragment presents pseudoTarget as a read of an existing event object that yields either a CSSPseudoElement or null, with Event.target unchanged — no constructor, no method call, no parsing step and no permission an author can fail, and an event type outside the table at #supported-event-types simply never populates the property (a coverage gap recorded under inputs and compatibility, not an exception). Neither css-pseudo-4 §7.1 nor the ChromeStatus record re-fetched 2026-10-06 defines throwing behaviour for it.

context.rationale: This fragment fixes where the surface exists at the API level: the property rides on UIEvent, AnimationEvent and TransitionEvent instances, and is non-null only when the event was dispatched on a pseudo-element, so a reader can tell from it alone whether a given handler will see a value. The platform and release side of context — Chrome 147 on desktop, Android and WebView, enabled by default — is in #at-a-glance, cited under lifecycle.

lifecycle.rationale: #at-a-glance states the release position — 'Shipped in Chrome 147 (desktop, Android, WebView)', 'Status: Enabled by default', and the linked ChromeStatus feature id 5179328935624704. The record re-fetched 2026-10-06 agrees on the 147 milestones but not on the status wording; both sides are recorded in notes and neither is adjudicated here.

examples.rationale: A runnable <pre><code> block already on the page, about this property: a click listener on document.querySelector('.box') that branches on event.pseudoTarget !== null and logs event.pseudoTarget.type (e.g. '::after') and event.pseudoTarget.element, with an else branch for a click on the element itself. A second block in the same section, under the 'Reacting to a transition on ::before' subheading (left without an id, since no selector points at it), does the same for a transitionend listener testing event.pseudoTarget?.type === '::before'.

compatibility.rationale: The fragment is a <table> of per-browser support: 'Chrome 147+ (desktop, Android, WebView) — Enabled by default', 'Firefox — No signal', 'Safari — No signal'.

securityPrivacy.rationale: #why-it-exists describes the whole disclosed surface: telling a handler that the interaction landed on one of the author's own pseudo-elements rather than on the element, replacing the geometry calculations and layout mirrors developers previously used to infer the hit. That reveals nothing beyond the author's own document — no new cross-origin, storage, identity or sensor access — and the page documents no security or privacy consideration. Stated precisely: the ChromeStatus record re-fetched 2026-10-06 still carries security_review_status and privacy_review_status 'Pending' with no recorded considerations, so this is 'no documented surface', not 'reviewed and cleared'.

notes: Every cited source was re-fetched on 2026-10-06 and checked against the page; the divergences below state both sides and adjudicate neither. (1) Release status — the page's eyebrow ('v147 · shipped'), lede and #at-a-glance rows read 'Shipped in Chrome 147 (desktop, Android, WebView)' and 'Status: Enabled by default', while the ChromeStatus record re-fetched on 2026-10-06 reads browsers.chrome.status.text 'Proposed', is_released false, intent_stage 'None', flag false and origintrial false; the record's milestones do match the page (desktop 147, android 147, webview 147), so the two sides disagree on release state, not on version. (2) Specification — the page's #at-a-glance 'Spec' row and its see-also list name CSS Pseudo-Elements Level 4, while the same ChromeStatus record re-fetched on 2026-10-06 gives spec_link https://github.com/w3c/uievents/pull/413/changes and the css-pseudo-4 draft re-fetched on 2026-10-06 contains zero occurrences of 'pseudoTarget', 'UIEvent' or 'AnimationEvent' (it defines only the returned CSSPseudoElement interface, §7.1); the page does not link the uievents pull request, and since a cited source must be linked by the page no new citation was added — the divergence is carried here instead. (3) Returned object — the page states pseudoTarget yields a CSSPseudoElement whose type is the pseudo-element selector and whose element is the originating DOM element, which the MDN CSSPseudoElement page re-fetched on 2026-10-06 corroborates for exactly those two members, while that same MDN page re-fetched on 2026-10-06 does not mention pseudoTarget anywhere. (4) Uncited attribution — three .citation spans on the page name 'blink-dev Intent to Ship — Pseudo target on events, April 2026' in plain text; the page does not link that thread and the ChromeStatus record re-fetched on 2026-10-06 carries intent_stage 'None' with no intent URLs, so no canonical thread URL could be established from the re-fetched sources, no anchor was added, and the contract cites the ChromeStatus record instead — whose summary carries the same three interfaces and the same hover-event exclusion the page attributes to that thread. (5) Internal to the page rather than a source disagreement — the lede and #the-pseudotarget-property say the property is carried by UIEvent, AnimationEvent and TransitionEvent, while the #at-a-glance 'New property' row reads 'Event.pseudoTarget'; both statements are left exactly as written. (6) syntax is flagged in its own rationale: the page has no declaration grammar for this property (a read-only, UA-set attribute authors never declare), so the schema's forced syntax:documented for an implementation-sufficient claim cannot be earned honestly here; per coord ruling 2(b) the selector points at the closest honest fragment (#the-pseudotarget-property, which states the property's surface) rather than at inline code mentions dressed up as grammar. (7) Page edit for this unit was ids only, and where the ids sit is a measured refinement of the batch's heading-id rule: an id on the <h2> of a section whose first child is an <h3> resolves to an EMPTY fragment (the slice ends at that next heading — validate-artifacts rejected such an id on the 'shape of the API' h2 with 'has less than 40 characters of substantive text', and the same for the 'example' h2), so the ids for those two sections sit on the subsection headings that carry the content. Six ids were added, every one referenced by a selector or named in a rationale above: #at-a-glance and #why-it-exists and #browser-support on <h2> headings, #the-pseudotarget-property, #supported-event-types and #detecting-a-click-on-after on <h3> headings. The see-also heading and the 'Reacting to a transition on ::before' subheading deliberately carry no id because no selector points at them (the latter is named in the examples rationale as prose only). The page's two existing <pre><code> blocks were left untouched — no example block was added, no prose, structure or styling changed.
